near_miss.lead: Lying/lodging during the night: lagu / lágo with nottina / nótt; лежащю with нощь
near_miss.why_not: Both contain cognate lie and night vocabulary, but ordinary chronological lodging reports supply no distinctive formula or poetic function. The Homeric partner has a different verb and contrasts land with sea.

near_miss.lead: Co-occurring wife, daughter, sister and son terms
near_miss.why_not: The Norse and Irish witnesses describe specific genealogies; the Russian witnesses have different family relations, and the Vedic daughter/sister phrase personifies a ritual girdle. No shared relational formula follows from the cognate kinship nouns.

near_miss.lead: Poetic making and doing a great deed
near_miss.why_not: Norse orti governs flocc; mesti qualifies vinr. Greek great work and work a work cannot be assembled from these separate Norse constituents.

near_miss.lead: Midnight: miðri nott and νύκτα μέσην
near_miss.why_not: The cognate middle/night collocation crosses two bundles, but denotes an ordinary time in a Christian supernatural narrative and a Greek naval plan. No distinctive inherited poetic context or marked syntax.

near_miss.lead: Sleep, night and the onset of sleep
near_miss.why_not: Norse going to sleep or people being asleep lacks Homeric sleep seizing a person and the sleepless-nights formula. Herodotus 9.44 describes a comparable nocturnal opportunity, but being asleep at night is generic narrative timing.

near_miss.lead: Hearing words: heyri orð and ῥήσει / ἀκούσαντες
near_miss.why_not: Corpus searches confirm ordinary hear-words expressions in Norse and Greek. In the slab Greek ῥήσει is instrumental manner, not the accusative object of hearing seen in Norse. Shared speech vocabulary does not establish a marked inherited collocation.

near_miss.lead: Hearing a person named / knowing a name
near_miss.why_not: Norse naming and recognition differ from Greek treaty in name, advance knowledge of war, and Irish explanation of a shield name. No matched two-root construction in the anchors.

near_miss.lead: Life and limbs: líf eða limar; lífi oc límum
near_miss.why_not: A genuine Norse legal merism, confirmed in wider Norse legal texts. Greek Ion 1403 has leaving an altar and binding arms, not life-and-limbs: λιποῦσα belongs to λείπω, not the life root. Searches did not produce an independent daughter-branch continuation of the merism; Old English life searches supplied no matching limbs binomial in the inspected hits.

near_miss.lead: Warm blood in battle: bloð / varmt
near_miss.why_not: No partner in this bundle continues the blood/warmth collocation. Corpus search found Iliad 11.266 outside the slab, recorded separately as a search lead. The Norse warmth mapping to worm is wrong.
The Greek repeated formula describes killing; the Norse knees support a bowl on an idol. No loosening or defeat figure is shared.

near_miss.lead: Falling at feet and placing something in the knees/lap
near_miss.why_not: Norse supplication and submission have no matching scene in the slab partners (Achilles in floodwater, pyramid dimensions, naval losses). Searching γόνυ with πίπτω finds Iliad 5.370, falling into a mother’s lap, and other unlike contexts; falling and knee vocabulary alone do not establish the Norse submission formula.

near_miss.lead: Bearing a message: bar orð versus ἀγγελίας φέρειν
near_miss.why_not: Comparable messenger contexts and cognate bear, with different nouns. Carrying/delivering a message is an ordinary productive metaphor; neither distinctive wording nor a second cognate component supports inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Standing up to address an assembly
near_miss.why_not: Norse assembly speeches offer a plausible traditional scene, but the Greek partners use establishment/alignment language, not a speaker rising. No shared verbal formula in these anchors.

near_miss.lead: Binding an agreement with oaths: sáttmál svardǫgum binda
near_miss.why_not: Search confirms this is recurrent Norse legal wording. Greek oath/bind-lemma searches inspected here instead return need/request homographs or renewed oaths, not a cognate bind-oath formula. Sanskrit slab partners concern blood-rain and a hero’s position, not oath binding.

near_miss.lead: Tongue and words: tungo / orðom versus lingua / uerborum
near_miss.why_not: Both nouns are cognate, but Norse contrasts prose speech with effortless verse from the tongue; Latin gives a physical account of articulation. They do not share a syntactic collocation of the two nouns. Wider tongue/word searches chiefly confirm productive Norse and Christian expressions, not an independently anchored poetic figure.

search_lead.cognate: Norse varmt (varmr, neuter singular agreeing with bloð) and Greek θερμόν (neuter singular agreeing with αἷμα) continue Germanic *warmaz and Greek thermos, conventionally compared through *gʷʰer- warmth. Blood nouns are not cognate; the slab worm mapping must be rejected.
search_lead.argument: In Sigvatr’s battle verse warm blood comes into the sea; in Homer blood rises warm from a wound during fighting. This is a matching thermal epithet in martial bleeding scenes, with renewed blood vocabulary. Worth review outside the slab-anchor measure, but bodily warmth is literal and could independently motivate both descriptions; no claim of established inheritance.
